title: Python Programming Foundations
project: Combine variables, arithmetic and output in a small finished program.

lessons.title: Your first Python program
lessons.objective: Use print() to display a message, and recognise a line of Python code.
lessons.example:
print("Hello, learner!")
# Output: Hello, learner!
practice: Read and run the worked example mentally: predict what it will print.
Edit the starter code to produce the expected output. Run your program and compare the result.
Answer the quick check, then save this lesson as completed.
lessons.transfer: Use a different input or dataset. Predict the result before testing, record what happened and explain one change you made.

check.question: What does print("Hi") display?
options: Nothing until the file is installed
check.explanation: print() displays Hi. Quotation marks describe a string in code; they are not part of its printed value.

print(learner)

check.question: Which line stores a number rather than text?
check.explanation: age = 12 stores an integer. "12" is a string, and you cannot assign a value to a quoted word.

check.question: What type of value does input() return?
check.explanation: input() returns text. Convert it explicitly when a calculation needs a number.

check.question: Which symbol checks whether two values are equal?

title: First Aid Foundations
project: Bring together scene safety, observation and a clear request for help.

lessons.title: Make the scene safe and get help
lessons.objective: Recognise when it is safe to approach and explain how to summon help.
lessons.example: Look for traffic, fire, electricity, chemicals or other hazards. Do not enter an unsafe area or touch someone still in contact with electricity. Your safety comes first.
practice: With a partner, use a pretend classroom situation to identify two hazards. Do not create a real hazard.
Write a short emergency-call message with a location and what you can observe. Do not make a practice call to an emergency number.
After a short break, explain your result without reopening the example.
lessons.transfer: Describe a new school scenario, how you would recognise danger, who you would call and why. Do not practise procedures on another person; this is introductory education, not certification.

check.question: A learner collapses beside a live electrical cable. What comes first?
options: Keep away from the electrical danger and get urgent adult help
Move the cable with your hand
check.explanation: Do not become another casualty. Keep clear and get urgent help to make the electrical danger safe.

lessons.title: Help someone who feels faint
lessons.objective: Distinguish feeling faint from an unresponsive emergency and choose safe first steps.
lessons.example: A person may feel dizzy, weak, sweaty or sick, look pale or say their vision is fading. These signs have different possible causes; do not try to diagnose the cause.
practice: Use a drawing or mannequin to explain how you would help a responsive person lie down safely. Do not induce fainting or lift a classmate’s legs.
Say what you would tell an adult if the person did not respond or was not breathing normally.
After a short break, explain your result without reopening the example.
lessons.transfer: Describe a new school scenario, how you would recognise danger, who you would call and why. Do not practise procedures on another person; this is introductory education, not certification.

check.question: Someone feels faint but is still responding. What is the best first action?
options: Make them stand and walk quickly
Help them lie down safely and get an adult
Give them food while they are losing consciousness
check.explanation: Help them lie down safely and get adult help. If they become unresponsive, assess breathing and escalate immediately.

lessons.title: Respond to a small cut
lessons.objective: Explain basic hygiene and recognise bleeding that needs urgent help.
lessons.example: Get an adult. Wash hands and use disposable gloves if available. Avoid direct contact with blood. Do not put yourself at risk to obtain a photograph or inspect a wound.
practice: Using a drawing, identify where a clean dressing would go on a small superficial cut.
Explain why embedded objects and heavy bleeding need urgent adult help. Do not practise on an actual wound.
After a short break, explain your result without reopening the example.
lessons.transfer: Describe a new school scenario, how you would recognise danger, who you would call and why. Do not practise procedures on another person; this is introductory education, not certification.

check.question: What should you do with an object embedded in a wound?
options: Leave it in place and get urgent help
check.explanation: Removing an embedded object can worsen bleeding. Leave it in place and seek urgent professional help.

lessons.title: Cool a burn and get help
lessons.objective: Explain immediate cooling and avoid common harmful treatments.
lessons.example: Only if it is safe, move away from the heat source. Get an adult immediately. Electrical and chemical burns require urgent specialist advice; do not enter an unsafe scene.
practice: Point to the safe cooling option in the illustration and state how long cooling should continue.
Explain to a partner why ice and household pastes are not appropriate. Do not use hot water or create a real burn for practice.
After a short break, explain your result without reopening the example.
lessons.transfer: Describe a new school scenario, how you would recognise danger, who you would call and why. Do not practise procedures on another person; this is introductory education, not certification.

check.question: Which action is appropriate immediately after a thermal burn?
options: Cool under running water for 20 minutes
check.explanation: Use cool or lukewarm running water for 20 minutes. Ice and household pastes can worsen injury or interfere with treatment.

lessons.title: Recognise choking and seek urgent help
lessons.objective: Recognise the difference between an effective cough and a severe airway emergency.
lessons.example: Someone with a partial blockage may still speak, breathe and cough effectively. Encourage them to cough and get an adult. Stay with them and watch for deterioration.
practice: Use written scenarios to distinguish an effective cough from inability to speak or breathe.
Describe how you would summon a trained adult. Do not rehearse thrusts, back blows or mouth sweeps on another person.
After a short break, explain your result without reopening the example.
lessons.transfer: Describe a new school scenario, how you would recognise danger, who you would call and why. Do not practise procedures on another person; this is introductory education, not certification.

check.question: A person cannot speak or breathe and has an ineffective cough. What does this mean?
options: A severe choking emergency requiring immediate help
They should be left alone to rest
check.explanation: These signs suggest a severe airway obstruction. Get immediate trained help and emergency services; follow dispatcher instructions.

lessons.title: Explain your emergency response
lessons.objective: Bring together scene safety, observation and a clear request for help.
lessons.example: Check that the scene is safe, call a responsible adult, observe responsiveness and normal breathing, and get emergency help when required. Do not delay urgent assistance to finish an activity or take notes.
practice: Write a response plan for a person who collapses in a safe classroom: who you alert, what you observe and what you tell responders.
Ask a teacher to review the plan. Discuss the difference between this introductory course and certified practical first-aid training.
After a short break, explain your result without reopening the example.
lessons.transfer: Describe a new school scenario, how you would recognise danger, who you would call and why. Do not practise procedures on another person; this is introductory education, not certification.

check.question: Which message is most useful to an emergency dispatcher?
options: A person collapsed in Room 2 at our school, is not responding, and I will follow your instructions
I know the diagnosis without checking
check.explanation: A clear location and direct observations help the dispatcher choose appropriate next steps. Stay on the line.

title: Machine Learning Foundations
project: Identify missing representation, privacy risks and limits in a model claim.

lessons.title: Meet a small dataset
lessons.objective: Describe a dataset and calculate an average using Python.
lessons.example:
import numpy as np
values = np.array([10, 20, 30])
print(float(values.mean()))
# Output: 20.0
practice: Predict the example’s result before you run it.
Change the starter code to meet the task and compare the output with the expected result.
Try another value after passing the check and explain the change.
lessons.transfer: Use a different input or dataset. Predict the result before testing, record what happened and explain one change you made.

check.question: What does a row usually represent in a simple dataset?
check.explanation: A row commonly describes one observation. Always check the dataset’s documentation.

lessons.title: Keep training and testing separate
lessons.objective: Explain why a model should be checked on examples it has not learned from.
lessons.example:
values = [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]
train = values[:3]
test = values[3:]
print(len(train), len(test))
# Output: 3 2
practice: Predict the example’s result before you run it.
Change the starter code to meet the task and compare the output with the expected result.
Try another value after passing the check and explain the change.
lessons.transfer: Use a different input or dataset. Predict the result before testing, record what happened and explain one change you made.

check.question: Why hold back test data?
options: To make training scores look higher
check.explanation: Unseen test examples give a more useful check of generalisation than training results alone.

lessons.title: Measure a prediction result
lessons.objective: Compare simple predicted labels against known answers.
lessons.example:
actual = [1, 0, 1, 0]
predicted = [1, 0, 0, 0]
correct = sum(a == p for a, p in zip(actual, predicted))
print(correct)
# Output: 3
practice: Predict the example’s result before you run it.
Change the starter code to meet the task and compare the output with the expected result.
Try another value after passing the check and explain the change.
lessons.transfer: Use a different input or dataset. Predict the result before testing, record what happened and explain one change you made.

check.question: Three correct predictions out of four gives what accuracy?
check.explanation: 3 ÷ 4 × 100 = 75%. This alone does not tell you which mistakes occurred.

lessons.title: Decide whether the evidence is enough
lessons.objective: Identify missing representation, privacy risks and limits in a model claim.
lessons.example: A dataset from one school or season may not represent another setting. Check how observations were selected and whether important groups or conditions are missing.
practice: Write a model note for a pretend plant-watering predictor trained only during a wet month.
Name one missing condition, one evaluation you would add and one decision that should remain with a person.
After a short break, explain your result without reopening the example.
lessons.transfer: Use a different input or dataset. Predict the result before testing, record what happened and explain one change you made.

check.question: A model tested at only one school should be described as…
options: A limited result needing broader evaluation
check.explanation: Evidence from one setting has limits. Broader evaluation is needed before broader claims.

title: Robotics with Sensors and Arduino
project: Distinguish a sensor, controller and actuator without wiring hardware.

lessons.title: Move a simulated robot
lessons.objective: Use a command to move a robot on a small grid.

forward(1)
print("Moved one square")

check.question: Where does forward(2) end when starting at (2, 2) facing right?
check.explanation: Facing right increases the column: 2 + 2 = 4. The row stays 2.

lessons.title: Turn before moving
lessons.objective: Explain why turning changes direction but not location.
lessons.example:
turn_right()
forward(1)
print("Turned and moved")
practice: Predict the example’s result before you run it.
Change the starter code to meet the task and compare the output with the expected result.
Try another value after passing the check and explain the change.
lessons.transfer: Change one design constraint and predict the effect. Test a safe paper or software model, record observations and explain the redesign. No mains electricity or unsupervised tools.

check.question: What changes when turn_right() runs by itself?
check.explanation: The simulated robot rotates without changing its square.

lessons.title: Plan a two-part route
lessons.objective: Break a route into movement and turning instructions.
lessons.example:
forward(2)
turn_right()
forward(1)
print("Route complete")
practice: Predict the example’s result before you run it.

check.question: Why trace intermediate positions?
options: To see where an instruction first changes the route incorrectly
To prove a physical robot is safe
check.explanation: Tracing helps locate the first incorrect instruction instead of guessing at the final result.

lessons.title: Connect the simulation to real robotics ideas
lessons.objective: Distinguish a sensor, controller and actuator without wiring hardware.
lessons.example: A sensor measures a condition such as light or distance. A controller processes the reading. An actuator, such as a motor, produces an action.
practice: Draw a distance sensor → controller → motor diagram for a robot that stops before an obstacle.
Describe one sensor failure and a safe response. Do not wire or power hardware for this activity.
After a short break, explain your result without reopening the example.
lessons.transfer: Change one design constraint and predict the effect. Test a safe paper or software model, record observations and explain the redesign. No mains electricity or unsupervised tools.

check.question: Which component measures distance?
check.explanation: A distance sensor measures the condition; a motor produces motion.

title: Research Skills for Student Projects
project: Use evidence to support a cautious conclusion and acknowledge sources.

lessons.title: Ask a question you can investigate
lessons.objective: Turn a broad interest into a specific, answerable research question.
lessons.example: “Plants” is a topic. “How does the amount of light affect bean seedling height over two weeks?” identifies what changes, what is measured and a period.
practice: Write a question about a safe everyday observation and identify the measured outcome.
List two conditions you would keep similar and ask a teacher to review your plan.
After a short break, explain your result without reopening the example.
lessons.transfer: Apply the method to a new question in your school. Separate observation from inference, give one limitation and explain how you would improve the evidence.

check.question: Which question is most testable?
options: How does daily light duration affect seedling height over two weeks?
check.explanation: The question identifies a factor, a measurable outcome and a timeframe.

lessons.title: Keep an evidence notebook
lessons.objective: Record observations consistently and distinguish data from interpretation.
lessons.example: Use columns for date, item identifier, measurement and unit. Record the method and equipment so another learner can understand how the data was collected.
practice: Create a table for three invented seedling measurements, with dates and centimetres. Clearly mark it as practice data.
Write one observation and one possible interpretation in separate sentences.
After a short break, explain your result without reopening the example.
lessons.transfer: Apply the method to a new question in your school. Separate observation from inference, give one limitation and explain how you would improve the evidence.

check.question: Which entry is most useful?
options: Seedling A: 8.2 cm, measured from soil to tip on 26 October
check.explanation: The entry identifies the item, unit, method and date.

lessons.title: Explain a result and its limits
lessons.objective: Use evidence to support a cautious conclusion and acknowledge sources.
lessons.example: Summarise the measurements that answer the original question. Use a labelled table or graph with units. Do not select only the measurements that support your preferred result.
practice: Write a four-sentence report: question, evidence, conclusion and limitation.
Add a source entry for a real reference you used, rather than inventing a citation.
After a short break, explain your result without reopening the example.
lessons.transfer: Apply the method to a new question in your school. Separate observation from inference, give one limitation and explain how you would improve the evidence.

check.question: A cautious conclusion should include…
options: A claim that the result applies everywhere
check.explanation: A useful conclusion states what the evidence supports and where uncertainty remains.

title: Cyber Safety and Networking
project: Describe how a device reaches a service through a network.

lessons.title: Protect an account
lessons.objective: Explain unique passwords, passphrases and multi-factor authentication.
lessons.example: A long, unique password or passphrase reduces the risk from password reuse. A trusted password manager can help. Do not enter a real password into a lesson or share it with classmates.
practice: Write a fictional checklist for securing a practice account. Do not include real credentials.
Explain how reusing a password can affect several accounts.
After a short break, explain your result without reopening the example.
lessons.transfer: Use a different input or dataset. Predict the result before testing, record what happened and explain one change you made.

check.question: Which practice best limits damage from one leaked password?
options: Using a different strong password for each account
Sending it to a class group
check.explanation: Unique passwords prevent one leaked credential from directly unlocking every other account.

lessons.title: Recognise a suspicious message
lessons.objective: Pause, verify and report messages that ask for money or account access.
lessons.example: A message may imitate a school or company and create urgency. Requests for passwords, verification codes or unexpected payments deserve extra care, even if the branding looks familiar.
practice: Draft a fictional urgent-payment message and mark two warning signs. Do not send it.
Write the independent route you would use to verify it.
After a short break, explain your result without reopening the example.
lessons.transfer: Use a different input or dataset. Predict the result before testing, record what happened and explain one change you made.

check.question: A message asks for your one-time login code. What should you do?
options: Share it with the sender after checking the logo
Keep it private and verify through an official route
check.explanation: A verification code can give access to an account. Branding is not proof of identity.

lessons.title: Trace a safe web request
lessons.objective: Describe how a device reaches a service through a network.
lessons.example: Your device sends data through a local network and other systems to reach a service. A router forwards traffic between networks; a server provides a service.
practice: Draw learner device → router → internet → learning server and label each part.
Explain why checking a domain name still matters when a page uses HTTPS.
After a short break, explain your result without reopening the example.
lessons.transfer: Use a different input or dataset. Predict the result before testing, record what happened and explain one change you made.

check.question: What does HTTPS alone guarantee about a website?
options: That everything on it is true
That the connection is encrypted to the connected site
That it belongs to your school
check.explanation: HTTPS protects the connection; it is not a general guarantee of the site’s honesty or ownership.

title: CAD and Digital Fabrication
project: Plan a safe prototype test and recognise manufacturing limits.

lessons.title: Turn an idea into a measured brief
lessons.objective: Describe a simple object using purpose, dimensions and constraints.
lessons.example: A design brief explains who needs the object and what it should do. For a pencil tray, consider pencil length, available desk space and whether sharp edges could cause harm.
practice: Draw a pencil tray with labelled length, width and height in millimetres.
Write one fit requirement and one appearance preference.
After a short break, explain your result without reopening the example.
lessons.transfer: Change one design constraint and predict the effect. Test a safe paper or software model, record observations and explain the redesign. No mains electricity or unsupervised tools.

check.question: Which dimension is unambiguous?
check.explanation: A numerical value with a unit communicates a reproducible dimension.

lessons.title: Understand a sketch and an extrusion
lessons.objective: Explain how a flat profile can become a three-dimensional form.
lessons.example: A CAD sketch uses points, lines and curves in a plane. Dimensions and constraints describe the intended size and relationships, rather than relying on how a drawing looks.
practice: Draw a 60 mm by 40 mm rectangle, then a perspective sketch showing a 10 mm extrusion.
Label which measurements belong to the profile and which describes extrusion depth.
After a short break, explain your result without reopening the example.
lessons.transfer: Change one design constraint and predict the effect. Test a safe paper or software model, record observations and explain the redesign. No mains electricity or unsupervised tools.

check.question: Extruding a closed rectangle adds…
options: Depth to make a three-dimensional form
check.explanation: An extrusion extends a two-dimensional profile through a specified distance.

lessons.title: Review a prototype before fabrication
lessons.objective: Plan a safe prototype test and recognise manufacturing limits.
lessons.example: A paper or cardboard model can reveal fit problems before material is cut or printed. Compare its dimensions and function with the brief.
practice: Make a paper mock-up, or draw a test plan if materials are unavailable.
Record one fit problem and one design change. Do not operate fabrication machinery.
After a short break, explain your result without reopening the example.
lessons.transfer: Change one design constraint and predict the effect. Test a safe paper or software model, record observations and explain the redesign. No mains electricity or unsupervised tools.

check.question: Why test a prototype against the brief?
options: To check whether it meets the stated requirements
To prove every material is safe
check.explanation: A test should compare the result with requirements and identify needed changes.

title: Video Production and Editing
project: Plan edits, accessible captions and an appropriate export.

lessons.title: Plan a short story before recording
lessons.objective: Use a simple storyboard to communicate one clear idea.
lessons.example: A short educational video works best when it explains one idea. Decide who is watching and what they should understand or be able to do afterwards.
practice: Draw a three-frame storyboard explaining how to organise a study desk.
Write a sentence describing each shot and its sound.
After a short break, explain your result without reopening the example.
lessons.transfer: Create a second storyboard for a different audience. Explain how you changed the sequence, framing or message and why. Use your own or permission-cleared media.

check.question: What is the main purpose of a storyboard?
options: To plan the shots and message before filming
check.explanation: A storyboard helps organise visual storytelling before recording begins.

lessons.title: Capture clear picture and sound
lessons.objective: Identify simple ways to make a recording understandable.
lessons.example: Use steady framing and suitable light. Avoid placing the main light behind the subject unless that is intentional. Check the screen before recording.
practice: Record a short clip of a non-personal object if you have permission and a suitable device; otherwise write a shot plan.
Identify one lighting improvement and one sound improvement.
After a short break, explain your result without reopening the example.
lessons.transfer: Create a second storyboard for a different audience. Explain how you changed the sequence, framing or message and why. Use your own or permission-cleared media.

check.question: What should you do before a long recording?
options: Record a short test and check picture and sound
check.explanation: A test recording can reveal problems early without wasting a full session.

lessons.title: Build a clear sequence and review it
lessons.objective: Plan edits, accessible captions and an appropriate export.
lessons.example: Keep clips that support the message and remove unnecessary repetition. The order should help a viewer follow what happens and why.
practice: Write an edit list for your three planned shots, including one caption per shot.
Create a pre-sharing checklist covering privacy, permission, sound and readability.
After a short break, explain your result without reopening the example.
lessons.transfer: Create a second storyboard for a different audience. Explain how you changed the sequence, framing or message and why. Use your own or permission-cleared media.

check.question: Which addition helps a viewer who cannot hear the audio?
check.explanation: Captions communicate spoken content and relevant sound information as text.

title: Smart Agriculture and Climate Technology
project: Plan how to judge whether a proposed change helped.

lessons.title: Observe conditions before making decisions
lessons.objective: Choose useful measurements for a simple growing experiment.
lessons.example: Water needs depend on the crop, soil, weather and stage of growth. A single sensor reading does not tell you everything a plant needs.
practice: Create a labelled table of three invented daily observations for a potted plant.
Explain which values are measured and which are estimates.
After a short break, explain your result without reopening the example.
lessons.transfer: Apply the idea to a different plant or growing condition. Record a prediction, one safe observation and a limitation. Do not use chemicals or powered tools unsupervised.

check.question: Which record is most useful?
options: Pot A, 26 October, 100 mL added, surface condition recorded

lessons.title: Draw a simple monitoring system
lessons.objective: Explain the roles of a sensor, decision rule and human check.
lessons.example: A soil-moisture sensor measures a property related to moisture. Different sensors need calibration and can be affected by soil and placement.

lessons.transfer: Apply the idea to a different plant or growing condition. Record a prediction, one safe observation and a limitation. Do not use chemicals or powered tools unsupervised.

check.question: A moisture threshold should be…
options: Checked for the specific sensor and growing conditions

lessons.title: Compare an intervention fairly
lessons.objective: Plan how to judge whether a proposed change helped.
lessons.example: Choose an outcome such as plant growth over a period or water used under comparable conditions. Record the starting point before the change.
practice: Propose a small supervised comparison using plants or clearly labelled fictional records.
Write an evidence-based conclusion that includes one limitation.
After a short break, explain your result without reopening the example.
lessons.transfer: Apply the idea to a different plant or growing condition. Record a prediction, one safe observation and a limitation. Do not use chemicals or powered tools unsupervised.

check.question: Which claim fits a small classroom trial?
options: In these recorded conditions, this outcome was observed
check.explanation: A conclusion should stay within the conditions and evidence actually observed.

title: Solar Energy Systems Foundations
project: Identify information a qualified installer would need before installation.

lessons.title: Follow energy through a solar system
lessons.objective: Identify the panel, controller, battery, inverter and load.
lessons.example: A photovoltaic panel produces electrical power when exposed to light. Its output varies with conditions; a rated number is not a promise of constant output.
practice: Draw sunlight → panel → controller → battery → suitable load; show an inverter only when an AC load requires it.
Label what each component does without wiring any equipment.
After a short break, explain your result without reopening the example.

title: Music Production Foundations
project: Create and revise a 30–60 second original instrumental track.

richLessons.title: Pulse, tempo and bars
richLessons.description: Keep an even pulse and build a four-bar phrase.
richLessons.objective: Keep an even pulse and build a four-bar phrase.

sections.title: Understand
sections.text: A pulse is the regular beat you tap along to; rhythm is the pattern of sounds and silences over it. Tempo describes the pulse in beats per minute. In 4/4, count four beats per bar. Four bars contain sixteen beats, regardless of how many notes you add. Start slowly enough to hear uneven spacing.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: At 80 BPM one beat lasts 0.75 seconds, so four bars of 4/4 last 12 seconds. Clap on beats 1 and 3, leaving beats 2 and 4 silent. Then clap on every beat. The pulse stays the same while the rhythm changes.

sections.title: Why this matters
sections.text: Listen before changing a setting. Predict what your change will do, test just that change, then compare the result. Write down what improved and what still needs work; a louder mix is not automatically a better one.

activity.title: Make it in Music Studio
steps: Open Drums, set 4/4 at 80 BPM and clap sixteen steady beats.
Create four bars with a clear first beat and some deliberate rests.
Listen twice. Count the bars without looking, then save your pattern.

check.question: What changes when tempo rises from 80 to 100 BPM?
options: The number of beats in a 4/4 bar
check.explanation: Tempo changes the speed of the beat; the meter and note pitches can stay the same.

richLessons.transfer: Without copying the pattern, rebuild it at 100 BPM and add a different rhythm. Explain what changed and what stayed constant.

richLessons.title: Build a groove with space
richLessons.description: Create contrasting drum patterns without filling every step.
richLessons.objective: Create contrasting drum patterns without filling every step.

sections.title: Understand
sections.text: A useful groove gives the listener both repetition and something to anticipate. Begin with a low drum on strong beats, add a contrasting response, then leave space. Syncopation can place an accent between strong beats. It does not mean randomly shifting every hit. Kenyan traditions have distinct histories; a classroom pattern is a technique study, not a claim to reproduce an authentic community performance.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: On a sixteen-step 4/4 grid, quarter-note beats begin at steps 1, 5, 9 and 13. Place a low hit at 1 and 9 and a contrasting hit at 5 and 13. Add a quiet hit at 12. Compare the groove with that quiet hit muted.

sections.title: Why this matters
sections.text: Listen before changing a setting. Predict what your change will do, test just that change, then compare the result. Write down what improved and what still needs work; a louder mix is not automatically a better one.

activity.title: Make it in Music Studio
steps: Build the sparse pattern before adding extra hits.
Make a second version with one off-beat accent and different velocities.
Save both versions and explain which leaves more room for a melody.

check.question: What is the clearest way to test the effect of an extra drum hit?
options: Change tempo, meter and instruments together
Compare the same loop with that hit on and off
check.explanation: Holding other settings constant lets you hear the contribution of the one change.

richLessons.transfer: Create a new response rhythm using different steps. Ask a listener to tap the pulse; note any point where the pulse became unclear.

richLessons.title: Write a memorable melody
richLessons.description: Use repetition and small variations to create an original phrase.
richLessons.objective: Use repetition and small variations to create an original phrase.

sections.title: Understand
sections.text: Pitch is how high or low a note sounds. A motif is a short musical idea that can return in a phrase. Try a small note range and a clear rhythmic shape before adding more notes. A rest can help a phrase feel finished. Use your own melody or a public-domain study; do not assume a commercial song is free to copy or publish.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: In C major, try your own four-note motif using C, D, E and G. Repeat its rhythm in bar two, changing just the last note. Leave a beat of silence before the next phrase. Compare a version ending on C with one ending on D.

sections.title: Why this matters
sections.text: Listen before changing a setting. Predict what your change will do, test just that change, then compare the result. Write down what improved and what still needs work; a louder mix is not automatically a better one.

activity.title: Make it in Music Studio
steps: Open Piano roll and write a two-bar original motif.
Repeat the motif in a second phrase, changing one ending.
Listen without the drums, then with the groove; save the melody.

check.question: Which is an example of developing a motif?
options: Repeating its rhythm with one changed ending
check.explanation: A recognisable idea can develop through a small, intentional change.

richLessons.transfer: Close your first pattern. Write a new four-bar melody with a different rhythm but the same note range. Describe why the new ending feels settled or unfinished.

richLessons.title: Match chords and melody
richLessons.description: Hear how a chord supports a melody rather than competing with it.
richLessons.objective: Hear how a chord supports a melody rather than competing with it.

sections.title: Understand
sections.text: A chord combines pitches; a major triad contains a root, third and fifth. In C major, C–E–G forms a C major triad. Chord tones are useful stable points in a melody, although passing notes can move between them. First match the musical key and listen slowly. A note that clashes may be a deliberate tension, but you should be able to explain the choice.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: Hold C–E–G under a melody that moves E–D–C. E and C are chord tones; D briefly passes between them. Now hold F–A–C and compare the same melody. Describe what your ear notices instead of judging by loudness.

sections.title: Why this matters
sections.text: Listen before changing a setting. Predict what your change will do, test just that change, then compare the result. Write down what improved and what still needs work; a louder mix is not automatically a better one.

activity.title: Make it in Music Studio
steps: Use Guitar or Piano to make a simple repeating chord part.
Compare the melody over two chord choices, keeping tempo unchanged.
Choose one combination and save a short note explaining the decision.

check.question: Which notes make a C major triad?
check.explanation: The root, third and fifth in C major are C, E and G.

richLessons.transfer: Make a new melody over your chosen chord part. Identify one stable note and one passing note in the new version.

richLessons.title: Turn a loop into a track
richLessons.description: Arrange an introduction, a main section and an ending.
richLessons.objective: Arrange an introduction, a main section and an ending.

sections.title: Understand
sections.text: An arrangement decides when musical parts enter, repeat, change and stop. A loop can sound flat if every instrument plays continuously. Create contrast through entrances, rests and instrument density, rather than just turning everything up. Start with a small, repeatable structure you can explain.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: Try a twelve-bar sketch: four bars of introduction, four bars of full groove, then four bars with one part removed and a clear ending. Keep the same tempo. Listen for a difference in energy at the section boundaries.

sections.title: Why this matters
sections.text: Listen before changing a setting. Predict what your change will do, test just that change, then compare the result. Write down what improved and what still needs work; a louder mix is not automatically a better one.

activity.title: Make it in Music Studio
steps: Bring a saved drum, guitar and piano part into Master Beat.
Arrange at least three clearly labelled sections with a planned entrance or rest.
Listen from start to finish and save or back up the project.

check.question: What makes an arrangement different from a single repeated loop?
options: Intentional changes in entrances, sections and texture
check.explanation: Arrangement shapes the listener’s experience over time through musical structure.

richLessons.transfer: Rearrange the same parts into a different order without changing the notes. Explain how the story or energy changed.

richLessons.title: Mix, export and explain
richLessons.description: Produce an original short track and evaluate it against a brief.
richLessons.objective: Produce an original short track and evaluate it against a brief.

sections.title: Understand
sections.text: Mixing balances parts so important details remain audible. Mute tracks to find conflicts, lower a competing part and avoid clipping. Keep headphone levels comfortable. Export a version, listen away from the editor and keep the project backup. Completion means you can explain your decisions; it is not a professional production qualification.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: Brief: create a 30–60 second original track with a clear pulse, a memorable motif and at least two contrasting sections. At the same listening volume, compare two mixes. Ask whether the melody stays audible and the ending feels intentional.

sections.title: Why this matters
sections.text: Listen before changing a setting. Predict what your change will do, test just that change, then compare the result. Write down what improved and what still needs work; a louder mix is not automatically a better one.

Export the track and keep your editable project or JSON backup.
Ask a listener for one specific comment, revise once and compare the two versions.

options: Creating a new track for a different brief and explaining your decisions
check.explanation: A new brief requires you to use what you learned beyond the worked example.

title: Songwriting & Arrangement
project: Create and revise a 45–90 second original song or instrumental story.

richLessons.title: Find your hook
richLessons.description: Create an original hook that fits a clear musical brief.
richLessons.objective: Create an original hook that fits a clear musical brief.

sections.title: Understand
sections.text: A hook is an idea a listener remembers. It can be rhythmic, melodic or lyrical. Start with one idea rather than a full song. A good brief names an audience, mood and approximate length. Use original words and notes, not a copied commercial chorus.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: Brief: a short school-club theme that feels welcoming. Try a four-note melody, repeat its rhythm and leave room for a response. Ask a listener which fragment they remember after a minute.

sections.title: Why this matters
sections.text: Listen before changing a setting. Predict what your change will do, test just that change, then compare the result. Write down what improved and what still needs work; a louder mix is not automatically a better one.

activity.title: Make it in Music Studio
steps: Write a one-sentence audience and mood brief.
Create two short hooks in Piano roll and compare them at the same tempo.
Choose one and record why it suits the brief.

check.question: Which brief gives the most useful direction?
check.explanation: An audience, mood and length give decisions a purpose.

richLessons.transfer: Write a new hook for a different audience using a different rhythm. Explain which decisions changed.

richLessons.title: Fit words to rhythm
richLessons.description: Place natural word stresses over a steady musical pulse.
richLessons.objective: Place natural word stresses over a steady musical pulse.

sections.title: Understand
sections.text: Lyrics have spoken stresses and syllables. Say a short original line aloud before singing it. Fit important words to deliberate accents, while allowing space to breathe. A lyric can be in a language you know well; ask a fluent speaker for help if the phrasing is unfamiliar. Avoid publishing private stories or other people’s words without permission.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: Write an original line about a familiar place. Tap four beats and speak the line in two different rhythms. Listen for where the important word lands. Shorten a phrase if you need to rush it.

sections.title: Why this matters
sections.text: Listen before changing a setting. Predict what your change will do, test just that change, then compare the result. Write down what improved and what still needs work; a louder mix is not automatically a better one.

activity.title: Make it in Music Studio
steps: Write two original lines with a clear theme.
Speak each line over a slow beat and mark the stressed syllables.
Try two rhythmic placements and keep the one that feels natural.

check.question: What should you check before forcing a lyric into a beat?
options: Natural syllable stress and room to breathe
Whether every beat has a word
check.explanation: Natural stress and breathing space help words stay clear and singable.

richLessons.transfer: Replace one line with new words while keeping the rhythm. Explain which syllables needed adjustment.

richLessons.title: Choose supporting harmony
richLessons.description: Compare two simple chord choices under the same hook.
richLessons.objective: Compare two simple chord choices under the same hook.

sections.title: Understand
sections.text: Harmony supports a song’s direction. Use a small set of chords you understand, and keep the melody audible. A progression does not become effective just because it contains many chords. Use listening and a clear reason to choose between versions.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: Try C major and F major under the same original hook. Keep tempo, instrument and volume unchanged. Describe which ending feels more settled. Note a place where the melody and chord tones align.

sections.title: Why this matters
sections.text: Listen before changing a setting. Predict what your change will do, test just that change, then compare the result. Write down what improved and what still needs work; a louder mix is not automatically a better one.

activity.title: Make it in Music Studio
steps: Build two chord versions in Guitar or Piano.
Compare the same hook over each version.
Save the chosen version and explain one stable note and one point of tension.

check.question: Why keep volume unchanged when comparing chords?
options: It helps you judge harmony without loudness bias
It removes the need to listen
check.explanation: Louder sound can feel preferable even when the harmony has not improved.

richLessons.transfer: Write a different hook over the selected progression and test whether the same chord choice still works.

richLessons.title: Shape verse and chorus
richLessons.description: Use contrast and repetition to organise a short song.
richLessons.objective: Use contrast and repetition to organise a short song.

sections.title: Understand
sections.text: A verse can develop an idea while a chorus returns to the central hook. These are useful structures, not rules for every tradition. Create a section map before recording. Contrast can come from rhythm, melody, lyrics or instrumentation. Do not label a random change as a new section without listening to the effect.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: Plan introduction → verse → chorus → ending. Keep the chorus hook recognisable. Try removing the drums for part of the verse, then bring them back for the chorus. Compare the energy at the transition.

sections.title: Why this matters
sections.text: Listen before changing a setting. Predict what your change will do, test just that change, then compare the result. Write down what improved and what still needs work; a louder mix is not automatically a better one.

activity.title: Make it in Music Studio
steps: Draw a section map in your workbook.
Arrange the sections in Master Beat with a clear contrast.
Count the bars and revise one transition that feels abrupt.

check.question: What is a useful reason to repeat a chorus?
options: To keep the central hook recognisable
check.explanation: Repetition can create recognition when it serves the song’s central idea.

richLessons.transfer: Rebuild the song with a different introduction and ending. Explain whether the central hook still feels recognisable.

richLessons.title: Record a clear vocal
richLessons.description: Record and compare two intentional vocal takes.
richLessons.objective: Record and compare two intentional vocal takes.

sections.title: Understand
sections.text: A good take starts with a comfortable voice, a quiet space and a useful recording level. Use headphones to prevent backing-track bleed. Test a short phrase before recording a full take. Never strain your voice or record someone without permission. Recording features vary by browser; upload an owned recording if microphone capture is unavailable.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: Record the same phrase twice at a consistent distance from the microphone. Compare clarity, timing and background noise. Choose by the brief, not by which waveform looks largest.

sections.title: Why this matters
sections.text: Listen before changing a setting. Predict what your change will do, test just that change, then compare the result. Write down what improved and what still needs work; a louder mix is not automatically a better one.

activity.title: Make it in Music Studio
steps: Open Master Beat → Vocals and record or upload your own short vocal.
Compare two takes using the same backing and listening volume.
Choose one take, align its start and save a local backup.

check.question: What reduces backing-track bleed into a microphone?
options: More microphone distance in every case
check.explanation: Headphones keep most of the backing out of the microphone; safe listening levels still matter.

richLessons.transfer: Record a different line on another day. Explain one change that improved clarity or timing.

richLessons.title: Finish your original song
richLessons.description: Export a short song and explain how you improved it.
richLessons.objective: Export a short song and explain how you improved it.

sections.title: Understand
sections.text: A finished classroom song needs a clear beginning, a recognisable idea and an intentional ending. Balance voice and instruments, check for clipping and listen to the export on another device if available. Keep your editable project and recordings. Only share work you own or have permission to use.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: Brief: create a 45–90 second original song with a hook, contrasting sections and your own vocal or instrumental lead. Ask one listener whether the words or lead are clear. Revise a specific problem rather than adding effects at random.

sections.title: Why this matters
sections.text: Listen before changing a setting. Predict what your change will do, test just that change, then compare the result. Write down what improved and what still needs work; a louder mix is not automatically a better one.

activity.title: Make it in Music Studio
steps: Combine your own beat, hook and vocal or instrumental lead.
Export a first version, get one specific piece of feedback and revise.
Keep the export, project backup and a short explanation of three decisions.

check.question: Which is the most useful revision note?
options: Lower the guitar in the verse so the words stay audible
check.explanation: A specific observation leads to a testable change and a clearer comparison.

richLessons.transfer: After a day, create a new opening for a different audience. Explain what you reused as a principle, not as copied notes or words.
